title: Ex 8.14 · Removing a set from a union
prompt: Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be any sets. Prove that $(A \cup B) - C = (A - C) \cup (B - C)$.
answer_format: A chain of lines, each a set (like A ∪ (B ∩ C)) or a statement about an element x (like x ∈ A or x ∈ B). Each line must have exactly the same elements as the line before; start from the left side and end at the right side.
hints: x ∈ (A ∪ B) − C means (x ∈ A or x ∈ B) and x ∉ C.
Distribute: (P ∨ Q) ∧ R is the same as (P ∧ R) ∨ (Q ∧ R). The condition x ∉ C must go with both x ∈ A and x ∈ B.
Each piece (x ∈ A and x ∉ C) is x ∈ A − C.
solution: Let $x$ be any element. Then $x \in (A \cup B) - C$ means $(x \in A \lor x \in B) \land x \notin C$.
By the distributive law this is $(x \in A \land x \notin C) \lor (x \in B \land x \notin C)$.
That says $x \in A - C$ or $x \in B - C$, so $x \in (A - C) \cup (B - C)$.
Every step was an equivalence, so $(A \cup B) - C = (A - C) \cup (B - C)$. $\blacksquare$

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses Section 8.3 (proving A = B), the definitions of union, intersection and difference (Section 1.5) and the logic laws of Section 2.6.

x ∈ A − C or x ∈ B − C
